_comment: Recording of live run 9 (status done); the plan is the model's own words.

steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget (budget year 2027), for P.S. 24 at 660 West 236 Street, Bronx.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, which is 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal and fits the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus solar within budget is estimated to cut 43% to 58% of annual use, which is 143% to 193% of the goal. It reaches the goal at the low end and fits the budget, with the high-cost case at the budget limit.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 66.6% to 84.9% of annual use and reaches the goal, but costs $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision after comparing that gap with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Every figure in this plan is a planning estimate with a range; no savings figure is certain.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: P.S. 24 is a flat-roofed elementary school built in 1953, with 115,325 sq ft of floor area and a 40,500 sq ft roof as entered by the user. The owning agency is the Department of Education.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Existing solar already on the roof: 228.2 kW. The city's solar readiness record also lists 228.2 kW installed, financed through a power purchase agreement (PPA), with estimated production of 249,879 kWh a year. No other existing renewables or efficiency work were reported, so the plan assumes none.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Annual grid use is 226,605 kWh. This is electricity bought from the grid, after the existing array. It matches the city's Local Law 84 energy report for 2024, which also shows an energy use per square foot (EUI) of 48.4 kBtu (thousand BTU).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city report also shows natural gas use of about 4,353,100 kBtu, so heating appears to run on gas. Gas heating is outside an electricity-use goal and is not counted here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Building footprints on the tax lot total about 40,497 sq ft across two buildings, close to the roof area the user entered. A footprint is ground area, not a measured roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record shows no landmark flag.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output range: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the standard 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof is 55% of the roof area after setbacks.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Panel density is 66 sq ft per kW DC.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft, or 115.3 kW (not metered). Backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed. Battery energy is 1,085 kWh after round-trip losses.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes, from NYSERDA data on completed NYC projects. Only 62% to 88% of predicted efficiency savings is counted, because the City's audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, DCAS, FY2022). The deep-efficiency saving of 15-25% is also a planning estimate.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The baseline for the goal is the 226,605 kWh the building buys from the grid each year. The existing solar array already lowers this figure, so the 30% cut is measured against what is left.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A standard efficiency package (LED and controls) is estimated to cut 14,050 to 39,882 kWh a year. Only 62% to 88% of predicted savings is counted, since the City's audited projects delivered that share. Whether LED lighting is already installed is unknown; any lighting already upgraded would lower these savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The roof area entered gives about 22,275 sq ft of usable roof after setbacks, which would hold about 337.5 kW if the roof were empty.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The roof rules do not allow a second whole-roof array on top of the existing 228.2 kW array. Only about 109 kW of free roof is left. This is a decision from the roof rules, not missing data. The first request for 337.5 kW was declined for that reason and the 109 kW size was used instead.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A new 109 kW array is estimated to produce 129,802 to 142,640 kWh a year (about 136,223 kWh typical), using flat-roof tilt and typical-year weather.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The new array alone is about 60% of annual grid use. Surplus solar is zero, so nothing flows to the grid uncredited.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Electricity price is a New York commercial average of $0.1981 to $0.2418 per kWh ($0.222 typical), not this building's own tariff. Annual savings from the new array are estimated at $25,714 to $34,490 (about $30,242 typical).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The city's solar readiness record gives no roof condition or roof age, and the year the roof was last replaced was not provided. Roof area, condition and age should be verified by an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A, efficiency only: reduces 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use (21% to 59% of the goal). Upfront $39,769 to $136,643; net cost the same; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years; within budget (14% to 34% of it); no outage backup. Does not reach the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency plus 70.2 kW of new solar: reduces 43% to 58% of annual use (143% to 193% of the goal). Upfront $217,212 to $400,000; net cost $163,979 to $320,993; simple payback 5.2 to 16.6 years; within budget (54% to 100% of it); no outage backup. Reaches the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, deeper efficiency, 109.3 kW of solar and a 1,085 kWh battery: reduces 66.6% to 84.9% of annual use (222% to 283% of the goal). Upfront $918,120 to $1,464,693; net cost $657,504 to $1,077,359; simple payback 14.1 to 36.0 years; outage backup 8.0 to 9.4 hours. Reaches the goal, but costs $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget. Meeting the goal this way may take more than the amount set aside.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The goal can already be reached by Scenario B alone, so the battery and deeper efficiency in Scenario C are mainly for outage backup and extra savings. Payback is a simple payback, not the full System Advisor Model (SAM) analysis. The model treats the capital budget as one total upfront amount.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency package: typical range $39,769 to $136,643; the median of similar NYC projects is about $87,016. Priced per kWh saved from completed NYC public-sector projects (NYSERDA data), middle half of similar projects.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, 70.2 kW of new rooftop solar: typical range $177,443 to $263,357; the median of similar NYC projects is about $210,573. Priced at $2,528 to $3,752 per kW, the middle half of 239 completed NYC projects of 100 to 500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data). The array is capped so the high-cost case fits the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B total: upfront typical range $217,212 to $400,000; the median of similar NYC projects is about $297,590. With the federal credit counted, net cost is $163,979 to $320,993, median about $234,418. Without the credit, net cost equals upfront cost.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Federal elective pay (direct payment of the solar credit to governmental entities) is listed as open, with solar required to be in service by 2027-12-31. Whether this school or agency qualifies is not confirmed. It is counted in net cost as a credit of $53,233 to $79,007 for Scenario B, but the deadline is close to the 2027 budget year and eligibility needs confirming.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario C battery (1,085 kWh): typical range $592,410 to $881,020; the median of similar NYC projects is about $745,395. Priced at $546 to $812 per kWh from NYSERDA data on 56 NYC storage projects. Scenario C solar is $276,310 to $410,094 and its efficiency package $49,400 to $173,579.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Left out of net cost: the NYSERDA NY-Sun commercial solar incentive, because its current status could not be read from an official page (check its dashboard in a browser), and the NYC Solar Schools program, because it is not known whether this building is in line (ask DCAS or the SCA).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYC Solar Schools program reports 130 completed school-roof installations under power purchase agreements; it is a possible no-capital route for added solar on this roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: None of these totals include roof repair or replacement. The roof's age and condition are unknown, so a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: confirm the floor area, the roof area, the capital budget year and amount, the tariff on a bill, and the roof's last replacement year.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a structural engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) analysis and a roof condition survey before any solar is added.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: LED lighting and controls, after checking what is already installed. Only 62% to 88% of predicted savings is counted.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and Con Edison interconnection application, with a licensed electrician and FDNY rooftop access review, plus approval through the owning agency and coordination with the owner of the existing array.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation of about 70 kW (budget-capped) up to 109 kW of free roof, in service before 2027-12-31 if the federal credit is to be counted.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery (if the owner extends the budget), commissioning, and checking results against utility bills.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C is estimated to give 8.0 to 9.4 hours of backup for the critical loads, emergency lighting and communications.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft (115.3 kW), with 8 hours of backup assumed and a 1,085 kWh battery. A metered critical-load list could change the battery size and its cost.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: FEMA's current map places the address in zone X, minimal flood hazard. Only the flood zone was read; heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A licensed structural engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) must analyze the roof. This plan cannot certify that the roof can hold more panels.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Also required: a roof condition survey, a licensed electrician, an FDNY rooftop access review, and a Con Edison interconnection review.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: As a Department of Education school, approval runs through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the School Construction Authority. The existing array is financed through a power purchase agreement, so its owner should be consulted before more panels are added.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: NYC sustainable roof rules (Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019) require solar, a green roof or both when a roof gets a major renovation. A roof replacement before solar would trigger them.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: No landmark flag and no special flood zone were found, so no Landmarks Preservation Commission or flood-zone review is added.
claims.label: FACT

sections.title: Path to net-zero and learning resources

claims.text: The goal can be met on electricity alone, but heating runs on natural gas. Reaching net-zero would also need heating to move off gas, which is not modeled here.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Floor area differs: the user entered 115,325 sq ft, which also matches the city's energy report. The city's tax-lot record shows 135,600 sq ft. The user's figure is the working figure; please confirm. The tax-lot record also lists the address as West 235 Street, which could be another frontage of the same lot.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The electricity price is the New York commercial average, not this building's tariff. The tariff must be confirmed on a bill; several Con Edison general-service tariffs are candidates and none is chosen here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The incentive list is kept by a person and each official page is re-checked. Two programs came back uncertain and are left out of net cost. Federal credit eligibility for this agency is unconfirmed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Not provided: the year the roof was replaced, roof condition, lighting type, cooling type, controls, critical load and backup hours, and the goal type. Battery size and outage hours rest on estimates, so confidence is low. Heating fuel appears to be gas, outside this goal.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency savings percents are planning estimates, so efficiency results carry low confidence. Cost figures are benchmarks from similar NYC projects, not quotes.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how to cut grid electricity another 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget. The plan estimates the goal can be reached within budget. Efficiency plus a new array on the free part of the roof is estimated to cut grid use by about 43% to 58%, for a typical cost range of $217,212 to $400,000. Efficiency alone is estimated to reach only 6% to 18%, so it falls short. The building already has a 228 kW solar array, and the 226,605 kWh figure is electricity bought from the grid after that array. Only about 109 kW of roof is still free, so this was a decision from the roof rules, not missing data. The full path with a backup battery is estimated at $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget, and the first two options give no outage backup. Next, have a structural engineer and roofer confirm the roof area and condition, and ask the city school agencies whether this building is already in line for more solar.
